title: The East India Company as a conquering state
paragraphs: The East India Company became a territorial power in India by war and by treaty, not by a single grant. At Plassey, on 23 June 1757, a short battle was decided by the defection of Mir Jafar. After Buxar, the grant of the Bengal diwani in 1765 gave the Company the land revenue of Bengal, Bihar, and Orissa. That revenue paid for further wars: against Mysore, the Marathas, the Rohillas, Nepal, Burma, Afghanistan, Sindh, and the Sikh kingdom, and for the suppression of the Polygars in the south. The geography is a sequence of forts, battlefields, and annexed courts, among them Srirangapatna, Assaye, Miani, and Ferozeshah, rather than a single moving frontier.

Annexation under an administrative rule is mapped separately from annexation by battle, but it is the same process of taking territory. Under Dalhousie, the doctrine of lapse treated a principality without an heir whom the Company recognised as forfeit. Satara, Jhansi, and Nagpur were taken on that ground. Awadh was annexed in 1856 on a charge of misgovernment, not under the doctrine of lapse. The rebellion of 1857, which followed these annexations, is a separate layer.

title: The rebellion of 1857 and colonial reprisal
paragraphs: The rebellion began with the sepoys at Meerut on 10 May 1857 and reached Delhi the next day. Over the following months it drew in soldiers of the Bengal Army, landholders, peasants, and the Mughal court, in different combinations at Delhi, Kanpur, Lucknow, Jhansi, and in the countryside of Awadh and the Doab. The Company called it a mutiny. A later Indian nationalist tradition called it the first war of independence. Neither description covers the whole. It was a mutiny in the army that became a political rebellion, supported in some districts and opposed in others, including by Indians.

The reconquest was, in several places, conducted as reprisal. At Kanpur, after European women and children were killed at the Bibighar, British forces used summary execution and collective punishment. Delhi was stormed in September 1857. Villages in the Doab were burned. There is no single defensible total of the dead. European civilian deaths, Indian deaths in the capture of the cities, and rural killings that were never enumerated were recorded by different parties for different purposes. In 1858 the Crown abolished the Company’s rule in India. That constitutional change is not a measure of the killing.

title: Tribal and peasant resistance, and colonial campaigns in the hills
paragraphs: The risings in this layer did not share one programme. In 1855 Sidhu and Kanhu Murmu led the Santhal hul from Bhognadih against moneylenders, landlords, and the Company’s administration. Birsa Munda’s ulgulan in Chotanagpur, in 1899–1900, was directed at landlords, Christian missions, and the colonial state. Alluri Sitarama Raju’s rebellion in the Rampa Agency hills, in 1922–24, followed forest laws that restricted shifting cultivation. The Mappila rebellion in Malabar in 1921 began as a tenancy and Khilafat agitation and became, in places, an attack on Hindus. Prisoners being transported by the authorities died of suffocation in a closed railway wagon. Other entries are colonial campaigns rather than rebellions against the Company or the Crown: the Anglo-Khasi war, the Lushai hills expeditions, and the Anglo-Manipur war of 1891 sit here with the Paika, Kol, Bastar, and Kuki risings. What they share is a geography of hill and forest that the administration of the plains did not continuously control.

On the agricultural plains the recorded conflicts are over rent, debt, and crops that cultivators were forced to grow. Indigo growers in Bengal refused the planters in 1859–60. Tenants in Pabna organised against rent increases in the 1870s. In 1875, Deccan cultivators attacked moneylenders. At Champaran in 1917, the obligation to grow indigo on a portion of the holding was the occasion of Gandhi’s first political campaign in India. The Telangana rebellion of 1946–47 was a Communist-led war against landlords in Hyderabad state, and it continued for a short time after independence. These campaigns are plotted together because they were rural. They were not one movement.

title: Colonial massacre and the killings of 1946–47
paragraphs: Several of these events were killings carried out by colonial forces. At Malerkotla in January 1872, Namdhari prisoners were blown from guns without trial. On 13 April 1919, troops under Brigadier-General Dyer fired on a crowd in Jallianwala Bagh, a walled ground in Amritsar with few exits. The Hunter Committee reported 379 dead. The inquiry conducted for the Indian National Congress put the figure at about 1,000 to 1,500. Both numbers are recorded. They are not averaged. Within days, Dyer ordered that Indians using the street where a British woman had been assaulted must crawl along it. On 23 April 1930, at the Qissa Khwani bazaar in Peshawar, troops fired on the Khudai Khidmatgar movement, which had adopted non-violence. Official deaths were numbered in the tens. Local lists were much longer. In September 1931, guards at Hijli Detention Camp shot political prisoners; two died. The massacre at Nankana Sahib in February 1921 is a different case. The killers were retainers of the gurdwara’s mahant, and the dead were Sikh reformers.

The killings of 1946 and 1947 are placed here because of when they occurred, not because they were the same kind of act as Jallianwala Bagh. Direct Action Day in Calcutta in August 1946, the violence in Noakhali that October, and the Partition massacres in Punjab in 1947 were communal killings among Indians, during the transfer of power. The colonial government did not prevent them. Death tolls for Partition in particular are estimates with wide ranges. This map does not choose one.

title: Nationalist agitation and revolutionary violence
paragraphs: The layer runs from Vasudev Balwant Phadke’s rising in 1879 to the strike by ratings of the Royal Indian Navy in February 1946. It is more than one political tradition. It includes the partition of Bengal and the Swadeshi movement (1905–11); revolutionary cases and raids, among them Alipore, Kakori, the Lahore conspiracy, and the Chittagong armoury raid; the Ghadar network and the mutiny of Indian troops at Singapore in 1915; and the mass campaigns associated with the Indian National Congress: the Rowlatt satyagraha, non-cooperation, civil disobedience and the salt march, and Quit India. Bhagat Singh, Sukhdev, and Rajguru were hanged at Lahore on 23 March 1931. After the Congress leadership was imprisoned in August 1942, protest continued locally, some of it violent, including a parallel administration in Midnapore. The Indian National Army, reorganised under Subhas Chandra Bose, fought alongside Japanese forces in 1944–45. The naval ratings’ strike of 1946 began in Bombay. Congress did not lead it.

Non-violent campaigns and political assassinations are in one layer because both were aimed at ending British rule. They were not the same method, and the map does not present them as one. The rebellion of 1857, the famines, and the colonial massacres each have their own layer.

title: Famine under Company and Crown
paragraphs: Nine famines are plotted, from Bengal in 1769–70 to Bengal in 1943. A traditional estimate of ten million dead in 1770 is not a census. Later demographic research does not treat it as a reliable count. The Chalisa famine of 1783–84 and the Doji bara of 1791–92 fall in the same early period of Company government. Under the Crown, the large famines on this map are Orissa in 1866, Rajputana in 1868–70, the Deccan and Madras in 1876–78, the Indian famines of 1896–97 and 1899–1900, and Bengal in 1943. For 1876–78, published estimates run from about five million deaths to more than eight million, and the range is contested. During that famine, under Lord Lytton, grain continued to be exported under a policy of not interfering with the market.

The famine of 1943 is the one for which the evidence is strongest and the argument most developed. Amartya Sen’s estimate is about three million dead. Arup Maharatna’s reconstruction from registration data is closer to two million. Other scholars give other figures. The causes under debate include the cyclone of 1942, the war, inflation, the purchasing policy of the Bengal government, and the colonial denial policy adopted against a possible Japanese invasion. The disagreement is about the weight of weather, war, and policy. It is not about whether a famine occurred. These events have a geography — districts of Bengal, the Deccan, Rajputana, Orissa — even though a famine rarely has a single date in the way a battle does.

title: Transportation, detention, and the political prisoner
paragraphs: Two institutions of colonial control are mapped. Neither was a war of conquest. The Cellular Jail at Port Blair opened in 1906 to hold political prisoners in solitary confinement, in wings built out from a central tower. Transportation to the Andaman Islands was older than the jail. What this layer records is the jail’s use, into the 1940s, as a prison for opponents of British rule. In 1914 the Komagata Maru, with Punjabi passengers aboard, was refused permission to land its passengers at Vancouver. On the ship’s return, police fired on the passengers at Budge Budge, outside Calcutta. Official and Indian accounts do not agree on the number killed.

Beside conquest, rebellion, and famine, these are small entries. They are included because detention, transportation, and exclusion were among the means by which British rule dealt with political opposition, not only with armies in the field.
